brief.goal: Understand that forces come in pairs acting on two different objects, and spot the pair in everyday cases

big_idea.text: Whenever two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other at the same time; the two forces are equal in size, opposite in direction, and act on different objects.

why_it_matters.text: This lets you explain why a kick moves a ball, why a canoe moves forward, and why a released balloon shoots away.

the_why.text: A force is an interaction between two objects: when a foot presses on a ball, the ball presses back on the foot at that same moment. The arrows do not cancel because one arrow belongs on the ball and the other belongs on the foot.

objectives.can: Describe the two forces in an interaction by naming both objects and giving the direction of each force.
Tell apart a third-law pair from two opposite forces that both act on one object.
Predict the partner force in an everyday push, such as a foot kicking a ball or air leaving a balloon.

picture.text: Begin with a foot just touching a ball. Draw one arrow forward on the ball, labelled "foot pushes ball," then draw an equal-length arrow backward on the foot, labelled "ball pushes foot." Colour the ball and foot differently and place each arrow only on the object it acts on. Beside it, add a standing person: gravity downward and ground force upward are both drawn on the person, so they are contrasted as not being a third-law pair.
picture.standard: Separate-object force-arrow diagram (paired free-body-style force sketches): one

card.diagram_ask: Labelled force-arrow diagram of a foot kicking a football: place the foot on the left touching the ball on the right; show a rightward arrow on the ball labelled "force of foot on ball" and an equal-length leftward arrow on the foot labelled "force of ball on foot". Use different colours for foot an

needs_first.text: Recognise that a force is a push or pull and that an arrow can show its direction.
Know that a net force on one object can change that object's motion.

mistakes.mistake: The equal and opposite forces cancel, so neither object can move.
mistakes.why_it_fails: They act on two different objects; forces cancel only when equal opposite forces act on the same object.

mistakes.mistake: The ball pushes the foot only after the foot has pushed the ball.
mistakes.why_it_fails: The two forces are present together for the same interaction, not one after the other.

mistakes.mistake: Because the ball accelerates much more than the foot, the foot's force on the ball must be bigger.
mistakes.why_it_fails: The forces are equal, but the lighter ball has a much larger acceleration for the same force.

mistakes.mistake: Gravity down and the ground's push up on a standing person are a third-law pair.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Both of those forces act on the person, whereas a third-law pair must act on two different objects.

opening_question.question: When your foot kicks a football forward, does the football push on your foot too—and if it does, is its push weaker, equal, or stronger?
guesses: The ball does not push back because it flies away.
The ball pushes back, but more weakly than the foot pushes it.
The ball pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction.
opening_question.answer: The ball pushes the foot with an equal-sized force in the opposite direction, at the same time.

route.what: Show an unlabelled foot touching a ball and ask the opening question. Keep the two possible force arrows hidden while the learner commits to a guess.
Place three choices beside the picture: no push back, weaker push back, or equal opposite push back. Ask the learner to choose before any arrows appear.
Draw a forward arrow on the ball as the foot pushes it. Then draw an equal-length backward arrow on the foot as the ball pushes back; make both arrows appear together.

Ask, "Why do these arrows not make the ball stay still?" Circle the ball for one moment, then circle the foot, showing that each arrow is on a different object. Answer: because only forces on the same chosen object can combine as its net force.

Write the rule beside the picture: if object A pushes object B, B simultaneously pushes A with an equal force in the opposite direction. Name this Newton's third law; avoid suggesting that one force happens first.
Transform the same two-arrow picture into a paddle and water: the paddle pushes water backward, and water pushes the paddle and canoe forward. Ask which arrow acts on the canoe system.

Put two mini-diagrams side by side. On the left, foot and ball have one arrow on each object: a third-law pair. On the right, gravity and the ground's upward force are both on a standing person: not a third-law pair. Ask which diagram has forces that can balance on one object.
Show a balloon releasing air backward. Ask the learner to complete the missing arrow and sentence: "The balloon pushes ___ backward, so ___ pushes the balloon ___."
Set a short balloon-on-a-thread test after the explanation: predict the balloon's direction, release it, then explain the two interacting objects and their two opposite forces.
Return to the foot and ball and ask for a two-part statement: "___ pushes ___; therefore ___ pushes ___." Finish by asking why the pair does not cancel.

questions.question: A foot kicks a ball forward. Which statement best describes the force of the ball on the foot?
options: It is equal in size, backward, and acts on the foot.
It is smaller because the ball moves farther.
It happens only after the foot has finished pushing.
questions.explain: The ball and foot interact simultaneously, so each exerts an equal and opposite force on the other.

questions.question: A canoeist pushes water backward with a paddle. Which is the matching third-law force?
options: The water pushes the paddle forward.
The canoe moves forward because the backward and forward forces cancel on it.
The paddle's backward push has no partner force because water is not solid.
questions.explain: The two forces are on different objects—water and paddle—so they do not cancel on either one object.

questions.question: A person stands still on the floor. Gravity pulls the person down and the floor pushes the person up. Are these two forces a third-law pair?
options: No, because both forces act on the person.
Yes, because they point in opposite directions.
Yes, because the person is not moving.
questions.explain: Opposite directions alone are not enough: a third-law pair has one force on each of two interacting objects.

try_it.title: Balloon force-pair release
try_it.stands_for: The escaping air is one object and the balloon is the other.
try_it.predict: Before releasing the balloon, predict: if air rushes backward out of the neck, will the balloon move backward, forward, or stay still?
steps: Inflate the balloon and pinch its neck shut.
Point the neck away from your face and from other people.
Choose which way you predict the balloon will move.
Release the neck and watch the balloon move.
Say which way the air went and which way the balloon went.
try_it.observe: Air leaves backward from the balloon, and the balloon moves generally in the opposite direction, although it may wobble and twist.
try_it.question: Why can the balloon move even though the two forces are equal and opposite?
try_it.expected: The balloon pushes the escaping air backward, and the air pushes the balloon forward with an equal force; they do not cancel because one force acts on the air and the other acts on the balloon.
try_it.write:
“The balloon pushed the air ______.”
“Therefore the air pushed the balloon ______, and the forces did not cancel because ______.”
try_it.in_class: Pairs share one balloon. The board shows: “balloon → air: backward” and “air → balloon: ____.” At the end ask, “Why do equal forces not stop the balloon?” A class answer that says “they cancel” shows that students are placing both forces on the balloon instead of on separate objects.

leave_out: Calculating accelerations of unequal-mass objects with F = ma; it explains a related puzzle but is too much for this short conceptual lesson. [S1#12]
Detailed force diagrams with several forces, friction coefficients, or connected-object systems. [S1#13, S1#14]
Non-contact examples such as Earth and fruit, magnets, and electric charges; these can extend the same rule later. [S1#11, S1#12]

from_lectures.took: Use the kicking-a-ball puzzle to confront the mistaken idea that equal forces must cause equal acceleration.
from_lectures.left: Leave out numerical mass-and-acceleration calculations because this lesson checks identification of force pairs, not computation.

from_lectures.took: Use the direct foot-and-ball opening, then make the different-objects test the central way to defeat the cancellation and standing-person mistakes.
from_lectures.left: Leave out the extended apple-Earth, fish, rocket, and acceleration calculations to keep one picture and one core test in a three-minute lesson.

from_lectures.took: Use the idea of considering forces on one chosen object when deciding whether forces can affect that object's motion.
from_lectures.left: Leave out the car-wall and hammer-nail examples because the foot-ball picture already shows the same reasoning more simply.

teacher_talk: Conversational and informal Hindi tone, using relatable analogies and rhetorical questions to engage the viewer, interspersed with calls to action for likes and subscriptions.
opens with a direct, intriguing question about falling objects and everyday bodily experiences
asks frequent rhetorical and direct questions throughout to simulate a dialogue
transitions smoothly using conversational phrases like 'but now comes the big question' or 'wait a second, I have a huge problem'
pauses to prompt the viewer to think before revealing answers
begins with a casual greeting and sets up the topic by connecting it to prior laws

diagram.ask: A standard diagram of a foot touching a ball showing a foot, a ball, an arrow forward on the ball labelled "foot pushes ball", and an equal-length arrow backward on the foot labelled "ball pushes foot".
diagram.shows: Forces come in pairs acting on two different objects in opposite directions.
